title: "Dream Scenario" and the failure to commit to a genre

commenti.body:
I found it to be very funny throughout. The commentary seemed to not just be about cancel culture but the entire journey of becoming famous IE: the scene where the girl had a sex dream about him and tries to recreate it - has nothing to do with cancel culture but a different aspect of fame, as does the meeting with the execs and the initial reaction by his kids and students etc - I get if some people just don’t like the commentary, or agree with it - so of course they won’t like the film in that case. 

But to address the point - it seemed to me the genre was pretty clear, it’s a satirical comedy. It’s not a horror film. Maybe people are confused by elements/tones/imagery that are more associated with “horror” - and prefer their comedies to be clearly wacky and light-hearted. Or maybe people aren’t a fan of satires if they feel the subject has already been explored enough - but it did something with it I haven’t seen before so I thought it was pretty good.

Very fair points made!

I will say though I bring up cancel culture because the film namedrops it, I do think the main point of the film is the spontaneity of fame in the social media age. So I think you are dead on there.

But I definitely dont agree that its a clear satirical comedy without being a horror film. Simply because I find that for large swaths of the film, the movie has no goal to make you laugh or really find it humorous. My theater was dead quiet during the nightmare montage, the scene in which Paul is being used for exposure therapy, the dinner party, etc. And I definitely find that to be the intention. The movie is trying to make you uncomfortable, and not in the cringe sense.

The film seems to want to tackle both the levity and humorous elements of fame but also the much darker underbelly that lurks within it, and that requires the horror elements.

Which is why many reviews also cite it as a horror-comedy.

>Or maybe people aren’t a fan of satires if they feel the subject has already been explored enough 

I definitely think I fall into this camp. I just didnt find much new within the film despite its premise that felt rife for potential for me.

But regardless, I am happy you liked the film! I certainly enjoyed my time, despite the movie not living up to what I had dreamt it would be.

I find myself a bit out of step with most people re: horror/comedy - as I tend to feel horror and comedy are very close genres. I’m a huge horror fan though so perhaps I’m just desensitized to a degree, but I did laugh at all the nightmares and that dinner scene - simply because they felt absurd given the situation, but were played seriously. Which is a brand of comedy I personally enjoy.  However to give you a sense of where I’m coming from - I also felt midsommar was mostly a comedy. To me it seems like people like Ari Aster and the guy who did this film have a similar disposition. It’s a very particular type of humor though.

Its why I don’t think I’d recommend dream scenario to everyone. It’s not frightening enough to work without the comedy, so you’d have to find that specific brand of humor funny in order to get the most enjoyment out of it.

Now thats an interesting take.

As another huge horror fan, some of the absurd bits elicited a laugh like Nic Cage stomping through the room, but others just only aroused a sense of dread.

>I also felt midsommar was mostly a comedy.

Yeah lol that is definitely in the minority there. I found some bits and bobs funny, but as a whole I found that movie to be a clear horror film.

Ive heard similar things about Hereditary where some people found it to be an exceptionally dark, dark comedy. I also think thats a lil crazy but to each their own.

I saw this film when it premiered at TIFF and the audience seemed fully invested in the comedy of the film, even in the horror moments. I think a lot of the problem with genre is how one dimensional it is. Sure, it helps you get your message across more clearly if you're zipping the audiences emotions from horror to comedy because you'll have a more obvious perspective. But in a case like this, or *Sick of Myself*, Borgli's last film (or even *Beau is Afraid* and the other works of Ari Aster), I feel like the absurdity mixed with reality gives us elements of truth that are impossible when you "pick a lane".

You said in response to another comment here that you think it's wild to think of *Midsommar* as a comedy but that's exactly how the filmmaker has said he sees it; like a break-up comedy. I think the ability to see movies from multiple angles might make them less effective in terms of eliciting responses typical of the genre, but that also allows them the chance to give us angles we don't usually see. 

I, for one, am very excited by filmmakers who are blowing genre up. I feel like Tarantino's picking and choosing of different elements of genre was what sucked me into *Kill Bill* and turned me full-cinephile when I was a little kid. I think we're seeing a great resurgence of that kinda thing in the Greek New Wave as well as filmmakers like Borgli, The Daniels and Aster. That makes me happy.

I agree with this. I wonder if you've seen *Sick of Myself* Borgli's other film. It has a lot of genre bending elements as well with a good amount of commentary but it's still hilarious just like *Dream Scenario*. I feel like I echo this every 4th comment on movie subs, but I'm really excited to see what he gets up to with his career.

>You said in response to another comment here that you think it's wild to think of Midsommar as a comedy but that's exactly how the filmmaker has said he sees it; like a break-up comedy.

Sure I can see that. But I believe moreso in death of the author. 

Ray Bradbury famously argued that Fahrenheit 451 had nothing to do with censorship. So though Ari Aster may believe that Midsommar is a comedy, I think the vast majority of people, myself included, would typify that as a horror film.

Because as I said in my OP, genre is just a tool. There are no steadfast rules for what falls in or out of a genre. But rather they are just ways to communicate what we experience to each other.

Aster calling midsommar a comedy may be true to him, but if you were to describe midsommar as a comedy to other people, it would fail to accurately communicate what you experienced to the vast majority of people.

My whole post is not really trying to argue whether Dream Scenario is or is not comedy, but rather did the use of horror and comedic elements add to the film or detract. Personally, I didn't find anything novel or new in the satire or story Borgli presented, so I wouldve preferred he took a different route. One that leaned more towards the horror or the comedy, rather than the awkward middle ground.

Yeah my feeling on the film was just that I was horrendously disappointed by the 2nd act turn follow up from a fantastic 1st act set up of all the ideas. If you're going to set something up as interesting as "boring area man appears in everyone's dreams and gains celebrity" I feel like cancel culture is the most dull way of playing that out. I also felt like everyone started taking stupid pills in the second act while people's behaviour felt very sensible to me in the 1st act. I feel like the film was trying to discuss the mass psychosis of fame and the internet, but just ended up in bland/zany territory which was an immense disappointment to me.

Wow you really hit the nail on the head. That perfectly encapsulates why I left feeling so… unsatisfied. The ‘critique’ in the film amounted to nothing. Bad for person when get famous too quick? Hard to handle pressure of everyone else’s expectations and eagerness to turn on you? Yes, very true!

Exactly how I felt re: genre. What a fantastic concept that was introduced expertly — I really felt in Cage’s characters shoes and the insanity of him putting all the pieces together. But then as you said, we don’t take it to a logical further end in terms of comedy nor in terms of horror. 

Did I have a somewhat fun time with the film? Yeah.  But I leave with a queasy feeling about A24’s direction in light of some recent headlines about them in terms of opening up their commercial appeal. If that means more extremely down the middle, genre non-committal takes on otherwise crazy, out-there concepts, that makes me very concerned and even moreso, sad.

I don't understand how film enthusiasts can say that Nicolas Cage is a good actor. He's so beyond awful. It would be like a gourmet discussion group raving about McDonald's.

There seems to be a significant portion of the population who are essentially tone deaf when it comes to bad acting. Somehow that portion overlap heavily with film discussion enthusiasts.

Well I definitely disagree with this. If you have seen moonstruck, leaving Las Vegas, adaptation, Mandy, pig, bringing out the dead,matchstick men and many more you would see an actor at the top of his game.

Nicolas cage is not a chameleon. You can't force him into any role.

But when placed in the right circumstance, there are basically no other actors that can pull off his energy and charisma. He elevates movies like few other leading men.

He is constantly aware of the camera, his dialogue is forced and wooden, and he can't convincingly emote to save his life.

If he wasn't from an inordinately wealthy family, he wouldn't have an acting career.

You can have that opinion. I just feel bad that you are missing out on one of the most unique and exciting actors in cinema over the past 30 years.

There is a reason dozensof accomplished directors including David Lynch, Martin Scorsese, the Coen Brothers, Spike Jonze, Warner Herzpg and many more have chosen to work with him

I didn't give you an opinion, I described the factual reality of his acting.

I feel the same way about your list of directors. The only one on that list who is kinda good is Werner Herzog, but he's too self-conscious.

If you want a unique and exciting actor, there are many. Vincent Cassel, Gong Hyo-jin, Javier Bardem, Hugo Weaving, Rik Mayall, Robin Tunney, Ranveer Singh, Dustin Hoffman, Miwako Ichikawa, Ratna Pathak, Jean Dujardin, Clive Owen, Sherilyn Fenn, Gene Wilder, Luca Zingaretti, Larry Fishburne, Jim Carrey Luis Tosar... and thousands of others.

Stop wasting your time on actors who can't act AT ALL. Can't even clear the bar of GOOD.

> I didn't give you an opinion, I described the factual reality of his acting

I'm sorry but I don't think it's really worth discussing art with someone that can't even differentiate fact from opinion. Have a good day.

When I say Nicolas Cage is aware of the camera, that's a fact. You may be oblivious to that fact, but that doesn't change it. A tone-deaf person is oblivious to out-of-tune singing, but that doesn't change the facts of music either.

My opinion is that bad actors shouldn't be in movies and it is embarrassing when people discuss bad actors as though they are worthwhile and talented.

I haven't seen it since my test screening, does it still hard cut to that awful fake commercial skit to introduce the dream-entering device? Third act is a real shark jumper for me in general but that scene in particular felt like I was watching a bad SNL digital short

To me, the films greater strength is in the personal psychology of the character. His repression is put on blast for the entire world and then the consequences of uncorking that same repression also is. His pride and suppressed feelings of inadequacy turn him into a monster that’s beyond his control - and yet very much what hurts his family is the way he acts in waking life, not the dream world. I agree that the films message about technology is kind of pat and warmed over, but I do really love the personal psychology angle and in that sense found the ending moving - as he finally realizes, hopefully not too late, what he’s had all along.
If only Scorsese had told him he's "aware of the camera", Cage would have realized he's doing Objective Bad Acting

>I also felt like everyone started taking stupid pills in the second act while people's behaviour felt very human to me in the 1st act. 

This was my major gripe with a film I otherwise enjoyed a lot. The hate everyone poured on him was way over the top and nonsensical. It's a metaphor, sure, I get it, but how about you toss some people in there that react reasonably to Cage's character, rather than everyone somehow believing he's actually tormenting them in reality.
Yeah precisely, like he should have had people willing to defend him - people ARE capable of separating dreams and reality.

I can say my feelings were not mixed. It was not a great movie to me. 

I think it was a weird move to make Paul Matthew’s so unlikeable. At the end of the movie there’s not real commentary on cancel culture, just that Paul Matthew’s is a narcissist. Which annoyed me, because I kind of wanted some substance after the painful first act. 

Also the analogies were just so elementary. Zebras blend into the herd, Paul Matthew’s is sticking out and now he’s being attacked. It’s so loose and breaks down at the first question. Why not at least try to play with some evolutionary biology. Why didn’t he lecture on ants at least one time? They have a collective consciousness communicated through pheromones (I believe, I’m not a biologist I don’t know). It’s like they heard the word “antelligence” and just crammed that into the movie for almost no reason, other than to remind us that Paul is a loser. 

Lastly, it was weird that there wasn’t a conversation about consent, when the movie ended with a new device where people can enter the dreams of random strangers. I don’t think I needed consent to be discussed, up until the end of the movie when Paul entered Janet’s dream. In any other movie or divorce scene that might be romantic and nice. But they spent the whole movie making Paul out to be a loser, that when he shows up in a dream without consent I just felt so gross watching it. I would have maybe been okay, had they not followed it up with the bookstore scene reminding us that Paul is a loser. So a loser enters everyone’s dream. Fine. The loser then gets out of peoples dreams. Fine. The loser then asks his wife if she’s dreamt about him, implying she has not consented nor been made aware of this. Also, shows his wife has absolutely no feelings for him. Then he enters her dream. I had to pause and ask if this was consensual.
I would agree that the blending of genres is exciting to see. Even agree that Borgli’s earlier film does a great job at this. But I just think he missed the mark here.
Might've ruined the movie for me unfortunately.

It’s such a truly awful bit that only a European director would stoop to. Just details the movie for such a non-payoff. Identical to the vomit scene in Triangle of Sadness. We don’t need a South Park scene in the middle of this movie.
It’s also such an unnecessary tangent. Just have him focus on her while he’s in the hotel bed and fail a few times then BAM he gets it and you do the sweet ending. Third act was such a fucking whiff

The other thing is, can we put a moratorium on using the Cranberries' "You're A Dream To Me" as the background music for every freaking trailer that comes down the pike for every self-styled free-spirited indie movie ever made

I mean they've used this song for almost every trailer ever made, it feels like...Choose a new song guys!!  The only other song that gets used for trailers more is George Thorogood's "Bad To The Bone"...Which was used 100s of times for movies in the 80s, 90s and 2000s...So much so, that about ten years ago the studios widely put a moratorium on it.  Which was smart.  They did the same with Van Morrison's "Brown Eyed Girl"...Which was also being overused...they should do the same with this...

I did notice that some people in the theatre seemed to take it way too seriously during the cancel culture parts. Like come on - that scene where no one wants him to get close to them in gymnasium was fucking hilarious!!
Preposterous thing to say lol. Nic Cage is one of the only actors that can be consistently entertaining no matter what he’s in. He does things with the form no one else has the balls to.

No one ‘picks a lane’ in real life so why should everything be so neatly delineated in film? 

Also I’m so surprised so many thought the film was about cancel culture. What about his inability to take action in his life?

I tend to enjoy films like this. They are descendants of films like Happiness and Being John Malkovich.
Yeah, he's amazing in Con Air.

You seriously have no idea what you’re talking about if you genuinely believe nic cage is a bad actor.

He’s funny as fuck in con air. 

Even if he does “bad” work, he still makes it massively entertaining as I said. There are a lot of actors you can give shit for their famous relatives - but Nic Cage is not one of them. Every great actor I know admires Nic Cage

While Cameron Poe is meant to have the occasional witty one-liner, he's meant to be cool and tough, not a joke. He is a joke in that movie.

Cage is just as wooden in Moonstruck. Bad actors have a dazed look, as though someone just hit them in the back of the head with a plank of wood. This is caused by them trying to:

* remember their lines
* ignore the presence of the camera
* hit their lighting marks

It's a lot for a stupid person to remember, hence the thousand-yard stare.

You have zero idea what you are talking about. Terrible actors like Cage have to be surrounded by great actors to have any chance of being passed off on a gullible public. Look at the cast surrounding Cage in Con Air, it's insane. Heavyweights all over the place, all to disguise Cage's mannequin performance. Cheesy action blockbusters don't normally have casts like the one in Con Air.

You said a lot of words that just don’t add up to much but a weird minority opinion on nic cages “bad acting”. Watch him in Leaving Las Vegas, adaptation, raising Arizona - then tell me how wooden he is. You seem to simply not like his performance in the films you mentioned, which is fair enough - he swings for the fences. But in no world is he undeserving of his status as an actor. Like I said, ask other actors what they think of nic cage, you seem to be of the mind you’re knowledgeable about what “good acting” is - but it seems very much your personal, uniformed taste. Which is fair enough, everything’s subjective. But most all people with actual knowledge about the field would definitely not agree with you.
Your punishment for saying Nicolas Cage is a good actor is having to watch his movies. Enjoy.
